sentences.text: Tupuxuara is defined by a large bone crest that extends from the back of its head all the way to its snout.
This creature possessed a toothless beak adapted for processing food without chewing.
Despite these large dimensions, Tupuxuara was slightly smaller than its closest relative, Thalassodromeus.
The genus was described by paleontologists Alexander Kellner and Diógenes Campos in 1988 after discovering fossils in the Santana Formation of Brazil.
The holotype specimen, cataloged as MN 6591-V, was found within this same formation, which is now referred to as the Romualdo Formation.
A second species, Tupuxuara leonardii, was named by the same researchers in 1994.
To date, there are five recorded fossil occurrences of this animal.
While earlier ideas suggested it ate fish or fruit, its lineage implies it was likely a terrestrial omnivore or carnivore.
Some hypotheses still suggest it may have been a piscivore preying on the coasts of modern-day South America.
Kellner initially assigned the genus to the family Tapejaridae within the superfamily Azhdarchoidea.
In 2007, Kellner and Campos placed Tupuxuara in the subfamily Thalassodrominae alongside Thalassodromeus.
Recent analyses indicate the parent group is Thalassodromidae, though some studies argue it belongs in the family Thalassodromidae rather than Tapejaridae.

Recent studies suggest Tupuxuara deliradamus, a species whose validity is debated due to its classification as a nomen dubium, should be removed from the genus Tupuxuara and placed in the subfamily Tapejarinae.
It is debated whether Tupuxuara deliradamus is a valid species, as it has been classified as a nomen dubium by Kellner in 2013 and by Cerqueira et al. in 2023.
